items.title: L8: How assessors score a Behaviour answer
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance and Success Profiles, GOV.UK
items.body: Departments usually score Behaviour evidence against a scale, often from 1 to 7, where the higher scores need clear, specific, relevant evidence of the Behaviour at the level of the grade. Scoring guidance normally describes what each score looks like: a low score for little or no relevant evidence, a middle score for evidence that is relevant but thin or only partly shows the Behaviour, and a high score for a specific, complete example that shows the Behaviour at the right level with a clear outcome. Practice varies by department, so treat the numbers as a general pattern. Assessors score what is written, not what they assume you meant. They do not fill gaps, and they do not reward effort or good intentions that the answer does not show. They also compare the evidence with the grade being recruited for: an answer that would impress for an AO role may score in the middle for an HEO role because it shows too little scale. Several candidates can tie on the same score, and sifts often use a cut-off. Where there are many applicants, a department may take only those at or above a certain score forward, which is why a middling answer can be as damaging as a poor one. Interview panels often mark each Behaviour separately and agree a final score after discussion. Because assessors may be scoring dozens of answers, clarity matters: a plain, ordered answer with the key action near the start is easier to credit than a dense one.

questions.prompt: A department scores Behaviour answers from 1 to 7. Which description fits a high score?

options.text: A confident answer with many general claims about reliability and commitment to the work
A very long answer covering several Behaviours briefly
A specific, complete example showing the Behaviour at the right level with a clear outcome
A well-written answer about a task that went smoothly, with no obstacles to overcome

questions.hint: High scores need specific, complete, relevant evidence.

questions.prompt: An assessor reads 'I was always a strong team player'. What will the assessor do with the missing detail?

options.text: Assume that a good example lies behind the claim, since the candidate has applied
Give the benefit of the doubt and add marks for the likely experience
Score only what is written, without assuming what was meant
Ask the candidate to clarify before scoring

questions.prompt: Why might an answer that would impress at AO level score only in the middle for an HEO role?

options.text: HEO assessors mark more harshly and use stricter language than AO assessors
HEO roles are assessed on a different set of Behaviours from AO roles
It shows too little scale or responsibility for the grade
It was written in the wrong format

questions.hint: Evidence is judged against the grade.

questions.prompt: Why can a middling answer be as damaging as a poor one in a competitive sift?

options.text: Departments may take forward only those at or above a cut-off score
Middling answers are discarded automatically before the cut-off is applied
Poor answers receive feedback and are given another chance
Assessors dislike answers that are neither good nor bad and mark them down

questions.hint: A cut-off excludes middle scores too.

questions.prompt: How do interview panels commonly score Behaviours?

options.text: Each Behaviour separately, then agree a final score after discussion
One overall mark for the whole interview, with no separate Behaviour scores
By counting the number of STAR stories told during the interview
By comparing each answer with those of the previous candidate

questions.prompt: Which feature helps a hurried assessor credit an answer?

options.text: A plain, ordered answer with the key action near the start
A dense paragraph that sets out all the details in one unbroken block
A story told strictly in time order, with a long introduction before the action
A list of Behaviour names at the top

questions.hint: Clarity makes evidence easy to find.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the 1 to 7 scale is most accurate?

options.text: It is set by law and applied identically in every department
It is used only for senior grades, such as SEO and above
It applies only to Ability tests, not to Behaviours
It is a common pattern, but practice varies by department

questions.prompt: A candidate believes that effort deserves credit even if the answer does not show the result. How are assessors likely to see this?

options.text: They give extra marks for hard work, even if the answer does not show the result
They reward what the answer shows, not effort or intentions alone
They add marks if the topic of the story was a difficult one
They treat effort as equivalent to a good Result

questions.prompt: What does a middle score usually indicate in the scoring guidance?

options.text: Nothing relevant has been written about the Behaviour at all
An excellent example that has only a small error in it
Relevant evidence that is thin or partly shows it
A candidate who did not keep within the word limit

questions.hint: The middle band means partial evidence.

questions.prompt: Why does the grade being recruited for matter when scoring?

options.text: All grades use identical evidence standards, whatever the role
Higher grades are marked more leniently because fewer candidates apply
Assessors compare the scale and responsibility in the evidence with the grade's expectations
Grade has no bearing on the scores awarded to an answer

items.title: L8: Comparing two answers to the same question
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A good way to learn what makes an answer strong is to compare two responses to the same question. Suppose the question is: 'Describe a time you changed how something was done.' Answer A: 'At the youth club the sign-in sheet was always a mess. I decided to make it better, so I made a new one and everyone liked it. It saved time.' Answer B: 'At the youth club, around thirty children signed in on paper each week, and the leaders spent about twenty minutes after each session matching names to the register. I suggested a tick-box sheet pre-printed with regular names. I drafted it, asked two leaders to try it for three weeks, and noted how long matching took. It fell to about five minutes, and one leader suggested a column for allergies, which I added. The club now uses the sheet every week.' Answer A has a vague Situation, no reasons, no sign of testing and no measure. Answer B gives a number, shows consultation and a trial, adjusts the idea based on feedback and ends with adoption. Both answers describe a real change and both use I. The difference lies in specifics, reasoning and evidence. When comparing, check five things: is the Situation brief and clear, is the personal role plain, does the Action show reasoning, does the Result have evidence, and does the whole answer match the Behaviour asked for. An answer does not have to be long to be strong. Answer B is only around eighty words; it is strong because each sentence does a job.

questions.prompt: Which feature most clearly makes Answer B stronger than Answer A?

options.text: It gives numbers and shows a trial, feedback and adoption
It uses the word 'I' more often than Answer A does
It is considerably longer, and length is what assessors reward
It mentions the children, which makes the story more human

questions.hint: Specifics, reasoning and evidence separate them.

questions.prompt: What does 'it saved time' lack in Answer A?

options.text: Any reference to the club or the leaders involved
A mention of a leader who supported the new sheet
How much time was saved, and for whom
A reason for choosing paper over a computer

questions.prompt: Which detail in Answer B shows Changing and Improving rather than just a one-off fix?

options.text: She drafted a tick-box sheet and shared it with the club leaders for comment
She counted the children who signed in each week and wrote down the totals
She tested it for three weeks and adopted it after feedback
She worked at a youth club for a long period

questions.hint: A tested, adopted change is an improvement.

questions.prompt: What does the allergy column in Answer B show?

options.text: She knows the children's allergies from working with them for years
She was willing to improve the idea using others' suggestions
She was told by the club's leaders that it must be added
She wanted to lengthen the form so that it looked more thorough

questions.prompt: Which part of Answer A is the Task?

options.text: The sign-in sheet was always a mess, which is the background
Everyone liked the new sheet, which is the reaction
It saved time, which is the claimed result
None is stated; it only says she decided to make it better

questions.prompt: Which of these five checks would Answer A fail most clearly?

options.text: Whether it uses I
Whether the Result has evidence
Whether it is about the Behaviour
Whether it mentions a place

questions.prompt: Roughly how long is Answer B, and what does that show?

options.text: About four hundred words, showing that longer answers always score higher
About ten words, showing that the shortest answer is the best
About eighty words, showing that strength does not depend on length
About a thousand words, showing that more detail always wins

questions.prompt: Which sentence in Answer B gives the Situation?

options.text: 'Around thirty children signed in on paper each week, and the leaders spent about twenty minutes matching names.'
'I suggested a tick-box sheet pre-printed with the regular names, as a way of solving it.'
'It fell to about five minutes once the sheet was in regular use.'
'The club now uses the sheet at the start of every session.'

questions.hint: The context and problem are the Situation.

questions.prompt: Why is 'everyone liked it' weaker evidence than 'the club now uses the sheet every week'?

options.text: It is shorter, and short answers are always weaker
It lacks the word 'I', so the contribution is not shown
It names a group, which assessors cannot score
It reports opinion, not a lasting change

questions.prompt: When comparing answers, which question checks the match to the Behaviour?

options.text: Does it have about the same length as the other answer?
Does it mention a number somewhere in the Result?
Does it have a title that states the Behaviour?
Does the whole answer show what the question asked for?

items.title: L8: Budgeting words in a written statement
items.body: When an application allows a fixed number of words, such as 250 per Behaviour, how you spend them affects the score. A practical budget for 250 words is about 40 for the Situation and Task together, about 120 for the Action, about 60 for the Result and about 30 for reflection or buffer. If you are asked for a single statement covering three Behaviours in 750 words, give each Behaviour its own paragraph, and keep each paragraph balanced in the same way. A common error is to write a long Situation because the background feels important. Assessors do not score background, so cut anything that does not explain why the action was needed. Other cuts include repeated phrases, adjectives that add no information ('very busy'), and detail about people who are not central. Where you must trim, remove words from the Situation first, then from reflection, and protect the Action. Do not use abbreviations the assessor may not know, but do not spell out every term either: write once 'Personal Independence Payment (PIP)' only if the role needs it. Check whether the limit counts headings and whether the application system truncates text. Many systems cut off anything beyond the limit without warning, so a strong closing sentence may disappear. Write in a document, count the words, paste it in and check the end. Never put key evidence in an attachment or a link unless the advert says that is allowed.

questions.prompt: For a 250-word answer, which budget best protects the Action?

options.text: About 120 for Situation, 40 for Action, 60 for Result, 30 for reflection
About 80 each for Situation, Action and Result, 10 for the rest
About 200 for Action, with no Result
About 40 for Situation and Task, 120 for Action, 60 for Result, 30 for reflection

questions.prompt: Which should be trimmed first when the answer is over the limit?

options.text: The Action
The evidence in the Result
The reasoning for each step
Background in the Situation

questions.prompt: A single 750-word statement covers three Behaviours. How should it be organised?

options.text: One story that touches all three Behaviours lightly
Two long paragraphs and then a short one for the third
A bullet list of the three Behaviour names with notes
Three balanced paragraphs, one for each Behaviour

questions.hint: Each Behaviour needs its own balanced evidence.

questions.prompt: Which cut loses nothing of value?

options.text: The adjectives 'very busy'
The reasons for key steps
The number in the Result
The verb that shows what you did

questions.prompt: What is the risk of a strong closing sentence at the end of the statement?

options.text: The assessor may stop reading before the last sentence, as most do
The system may truncate text beyond the limit without warning
It may push the answer over the limit for another section
It repeats the Result and so wastes words

questions.prompt: What should you do before submitting?

options.text: Type directly into the form and rely on its word counter to stop you at the limit
Write in a document, count the words, paste it in and check the end
Paste it in once and submit straight away
Send it to a friend by email and use their copy

questions.prompt: Where should key evidence go if the advert does not mention attachments?

options.text: In an attachment that the assessor can open
On a linked website that you control
Within the statement itself
In the covering email sent with the application

questions.prompt: When is spelling out a technical term in full justified?

options.text: Every time it appears, so the assessor never sees an abbreviation
When the role needs it, once, with the abbreviation
Never, since abbreviations always save words
Only in the Result, where the outcome is stated

questions.prompt: Why is a long Situation a common error?

options.text: It makes the answer too accurate for the number of words allowed
It reduces the number of Behaviours that can be covered
It is forbidden by the application guidance
Candidates feel the background matters, but assessors do not score it

questions.prompt: Why check whether headings count towards the limit?

options.text: Headings are always free and never counted
Headings are banned in all applications
The system might count them and cut the end
Headings are marked separately by assessors

questions.hint: Count the words as the system counts.

items.title: L8: Leadership evidence beyond a title
items.source: Civil Service Code and Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Leadership questions tempt applicants to list titles such as team leader, captain or chair. Titles are only a starting point. Assessors look for what the person did to guide others, maintain standards and set an example. At EO level, that often means coordinating the work of a small group, helping colleagues to understand the purpose of the work, being positive during change and speaking up honestly. A good leadership story answers these questions: who did you lead or influence, and were they under your authority; what did you do to give direction; how did you keep people motivated or on track; how did you handle a problem; and what was the result? A volunteer coordinator might write: 'When our usual organiser left two weeks before the summer fair, I offered to coordinate. I called a meeting of the eight helpers, split jobs according to what each preferred, set a checklist and checked progress each Friday. When one helper became overwhelmed, I took over her ticket sales and agreed a smaller role. The fair ran to plan and raised more than last year.' It shows initiative, direction, support and a result. Leading without authority is also valid, such as getting colleagues to adopt a better method. Weak evidence says 'I was in charge' or relies on being liked. Strong leadership often includes acknowledging others' contributions, which signals confidence and fairness. Leadership at EO level is not about shouting or controlling; it is about helping others do their best work.

questions.prompt: Which part of the summer fair story best shows leadership beyond a title?

options.text: She was a volunteer helper at the summer fair for several years
The fair raised more money than the year before
She called a meeting of the helpers
She split jobs by preference, set a checklist and checked progress weekly

questions.prompt: What did she do when one helper became overwhelmed?

options.text: Told her to try harder and carry on with the same role
Took over some of her work and agreed a smaller role
Removed her from the group so the others would not be slowed down
Ignored it, on the grounds that everyone was busy

questions.prompt: Which statement is weakest as Leadership evidence?

options.text: 'I agreed a smaller role with a helper who was overloaded.'
'I was in charge, so I made sure things were done.'
'I split tasks by what each person preferred.'
'I checked progress each Friday.'

questions.hint: A claim of authority with no actions.

questions.prompt: Can leadership be shown without formal authority?

options.text: It can, for example by persuading colleagues to adopt a better method
Leadership always needs a formal title, so it cannot be shown without one
Leadership without authority is expected only at HEO and above
Leadership without authority can be shown only in the voluntary sector

questions.prompt: Which quality is closest to what EO-level Leadership looks for?

options.text: Controlling others closely so that standards are kept
Helping others do their best work
Winning every argument to show direction
Being liked by everyone in the group

questions.prompt: Why does acknowledging others' contributions strengthen a leadership story?

options.text: It signals confidence and fairness
It lengthens the answer
It is required by the Civil Service Code
It reduces the leader's role

questions.prompt: Which question should a leadership story answer?

options.text: How long have you known the people you led?
What is the name of the committee you sat on?
How many meetings were held during the project?
How did you keep people motivated or on track?

questions.hint: The story needs the means of leading.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows being positive during change?

options.text: Helping colleagues learn the new system and showing how it helps
Complaining quietly to colleagues about the change
Waiting to see whether the change is cancelled
Ignoring the new system and using the old one

questions.prompt: What does the volunteer's Friday progress check illustrate?

options.text: Controlling the helpers closely so that no mistakes are made
Avoiding delegation of any tasks to the other helpers
Keeping standards up and people on track
Reporting regularly to a manager about the helpers

questions.prompt: Why is relying on being liked a weak basis for a Leadership answer?

options.text: Being liked is a negative quality in a leader
Assessors dislike friendly leaders as too soft
It lacks a number to show the scale
It describes a feeling, not what you did to guide others

items.title: L8: Decisions, honesty and raising concerns
items.body: The Civil Service Code sets out four values: integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. They shape how decisions should be made. Integrity includes putting the obligations of public service above personal interests and not misusing information. Honesty includes being truthful and open and not deceiving or knowingly misleading. Objectivity means basing advice and decisions on rigorous analysis of the evidence. Impartiality means acting in a way that deals with the public fairly, even-handedly and without favour. If a civil servant is asked to act in a way that conflicts with the Code, or sees something that breaches it, the Code expects them to report the matter. They can first raise it with their line manager or someone in their management chain, or with a nominated officer in the department. If the matter is not resolved, they can take it to the Civil Service Commission. A decision story is stronger when it shows these values in action. For example, an officer discovers that a colleague has been quietly relaxing a rule for friends, which treats customers unequally. She does not confront the colleague in public or ignore the matter. She notes what she has seen, speaks to her line manager and follows the department's process. The Result is not necessarily dramatic, but the story shows integrity and impartiality. Avoid telling stories in which you break rules for a good reason, since assessors may see disregard for process. Stories can also show accepting a decision you disagree with, once it is made properly, and carrying it out.

questions.prompt: Which value requires dealing with the public fairly and without favour?

options.text: Objectivity
Honesty
Integrity
Impartiality

questions.hint: Impartiality means fairness and no favour.

questions.prompt: Which value requires basing advice on rigorous analysis of the evidence?

options.text: Objectivity
Integrity
Honesty
Impartiality

questions.prompt: An officer sees a colleague bending a rule for friends. Which action best reflects the Code?

options.text: Confront the colleague in front of others straight away
Do nothing, since it is not her job to police others
Copy the colleague's approach so the rule is applied alike
Note what she saw, speak to her line manager and follow the department's process

questions.prompt: If a concern is not resolved within the department, where can a civil servant take it?

options.text: A local newspaper, to draw public attention
A trade association for civil servants
The Civil Service Commission
An MP's constituency office

questions.hint: The Commission is the external route.

questions.prompt: Which is a nominated officer's role?

options.text: To approve pay awards for staff in the department
To receive concerns raised under the Code
To audit the department's accounts each year
To recruit staff to vacancies in the department

questions.prompt: Why can a story of breaking rules 'for a good reason' backfire?

options.text: It shows too much initiative for an entry-level role
It is always dishonest, because rules are never broken
It is too short to be marked
Assessors may read it as disregard for process

questions.prompt: Which behaviour shows good judgement after a decision with which you disagree?

options.text: Delay carrying it out until the decision has been looked at again
Tell customers openly that you disagree with the decision
Refuse to carry it out because you disagree
Carry it out properly once it is made through the right process

questions.prompt: What does the value of honesty require?

options.text: Being truthful and open, not knowingly misleading
Keeping everything secret to protect the department
Always agreeing with managers to avoid friction
Avoiding bad news so that people are not upset

questions.prompt: Which action would breach integrity?

options.text: Asking a colleague for advice on a difficult case before deciding
Declining a gift that a supplier offered during a visit
Using information from work for personal advantage
Recording a decision and the reasons for it in the case file

questions.prompt: Why does the decision story with the colleague not need a dramatic Result?

options.text: Results are never needed in a Civil Service Code answer
It shows integrity and impartiality through the actions taken
The Code forbids mentioning outcomes in an application
Dramatic results are penalised by assessors

questions.hint: The values are shown by actions.

items.title: L8: Accuracy, data and Managing a Quality Service
items.source: ICO guidance on UK GDPR; Success Profiles, GOV.UK
items.body: Managing a Quality Service often involves handling personal information, so basic data-protection habits count as quality. UK data protection law, regulated by the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), sets out principles including that personal data should be used lawfully, fairly and transparently, collected for specified purposes, adequate and relevant, accurate and kept up to date, kept no longer than necessary, and held securely. At entry level, you are not expected to quote the law, but you are expected to behave accordingly: check you are speaking to the right person before discussing a case, share only what is needed, send documents to the right address, keep papers and screens out of view and report a mistake promptly. If something goes wrong, such as an email sent to the wrong person, the correct response is to tell your manager or the data protection contact straight away, so that the department can assess and, if necessary, report it. Hiding it is worse than the error. A strong quality story might read: 'I noticed that I had attached the wrong letter to an email. I recalled it, told my manager within minutes, phoned the customer to apologise, and wrote myself a checklist to check the attachment name before sending. The department logged the incident and no further action was needed.' The elements are honesty, speed, putting right and preventing a repeat. Quality also includes accuracy of records, so correct errors and note why. Compare this with 'I'm careful with information', which is a claim with no evidence.

questions.prompt: An officer sends an email with the wrong attachment. What is the best first response?

options.text: Wait to see whether the customer notices the error
Tell her manager or data protection contact straight away
Delete the sent email and say nothing about it
Send the correct attachment without comment

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the data protection principles?

options.text: Personal data should be shared widely within the department
Personal data should be kept indefinitely
Personal data should be accurate and kept up to date
Personal data should be collected for any purpose

questions.prompt: Which body regulates data protection in the UK?

options.text: The Civil Service Commission, which hears concerns about the Code
The Information Commissioner's Office
The Cabinet Office, which sets standards for departments
The National Audit Office

questions.prompt: Why is hiding a data error worse than the error itself?

options.text: It is slower to correct once it has been found
It prevents the department from assessing and reducing harm
It is more expensive to put right later
It is rarely noticed by anyone else

questions.prompt: Which habit shows quality when handling a case by phone?

options.text: Discussing the case with whoever answers the telephone
Checking you are speaking to the right person before discussing it
Leaving notes on the desk so that colleagues can follow up
Reading details aloud so that colleagues can help

questions.prompt: Which part of the example story shows preventing a repeat?

options.text: Recalling the email as soon as she noticed the mistake
Phoning the customer to apologise for the mistake
Writing a checklist to check the attachment name
Telling her manager within a few minutes of noticing

questions.prompt: Why is 'I'm careful with information' weak evidence?

options.text: It is too short to count as an answer
It is dishonest, because nobody is always careful
It is a claim with no example
It names no data protection law

questions.prompt: Which action is consistent with sharing only what is needed?

options.text: Copying the whole file to everyone who might need it
Forwarding the whole email chain to a colleague
Giving a colleague just the details required for their part of the case
Posting the details on the team board for all to see

questions.prompt: What does accuracy of records include?

options.text: Correcting errors and noting why
Deleting old records so that only new ones remain
Keeping errors in place for audit purposes
Waiting for a manager to notice the error

questions.prompt: Which pair of elements is shown in the example's response?

options.text: Secrecy and delay
Blame and apology
Delegation and avoidance
Honesty and speed

questions.hint: The candidate told quickly and truthfully.

items.title: L8: Working Together across teams and sites
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Many Civil Service jobs involve working with colleagues who sit in other teams, other buildings or at home. Working Together in these settings depends on clarity, reliability and good use of shared tools. Practical habits include agreeing who does what and by when, keeping a shared record of decisions and actions, sending updates before being asked, sharing information that others need rather than waiting to be asked, and responding to messages within the time you promised. When teams have different priorities, it helps to find the common goal and agree a plan that respects both. For example, a records team wants forms checked in the morning, whereas the payment team needs them by noon. An officer in the payment team phones her opposite number, finds that morning checks are possible if forms arrive by ten, and agrees a handover time and a shared tracker. After a month the number of forms missed at noon falls from several a week to almost none. The evidence is the proactive contact, the agreed arrangement, the shared record and a measured outcome. Weak evidence says 'I worked with other teams' with no description of who, what or how. Inclusion also matters: asking quieter colleagues for views, using plain language and thinking about different working patterns shows respect. Avoid describing other teams as the problem, since the Behaviour is about solving joint problems. If you are working remotely, say how you kept in touch, which can be as simple as a regular short call.

questions.prompt: Two teams want forms at different times. Which action best shows Working Together?

options.text: Phone the other team, find the common goal and agree a handover time and tracker
Send a complaint to her manager about the other team
Work around them without telling them
Ask her manager to change the other team's rules

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest evidence in the forms example?

options.text: The teams became friendlier with each other
The number of missed forms fell from several a week to almost none
The meeting was held in the morning
She was thanked by both managers

questions.prompt: Which habit helps remote or multi-site colleagues work well?

options.text: Sending updates before being asked
Replying only when chased
Keeping information until a meeting
Assuming others know

questions.prompt: Why keep a shared record of decisions and actions?

options.text: So everyone can see who does what and by when
So the manager can check up on what people have done
To avoid the need for meetings between the teams
To prove who was at fault if something goes wrong

questions.prompt: Which statement is weak evidence of Working Together?

options.text: 'I agreed a handover time with the records team.'
'I set up a shared tracker.'
'I phoned the team leader to ask what they needed.'
'I worked with other teams.'

questions.prompt: Why avoid describing the other team as the problem?

options.text: It is dishonest, as all teams share responsibility
It is rude, and rudeness is marked down
The Behaviour is about solving joint problems
It lengthens the answer unnecessarily

questions.prompt: How can a quiet colleague be included in a decision?

options.text: Assume that they agree, since they have not spoken
Decide first and tell them afterwards
Ask for their view directly and make space for it
Wait for them to volunteer an opinion

questions.prompt: What does a regular short call between remote colleagues demonstrate?

options.text: A practical way of keeping in touch
A lack of trust between the colleagues
A waste of time that could be spent working
A formal requirement of remote working

questions.prompt: Which element is part of the cross-team evidence?

options.text: Avoiding the other team
Waiting for instructions
Taking over their work
Proactive contact

questions.prompt: Why respond to messages within the time you promised?

options.text: It lengthens the day
It satisfies the manager
It reduces the number of messages
It builds reliability and trust

items.title: L8: Measuring the effect of an improvement
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Strong Changing and Improving answers show the effect of the change, but measurement is easy to get wrong. A reliable approach is to record a baseline before the change, make the change, and then measure the same thing again. Without a baseline, a figure after the change means little. If a team handled 40 cases a day before the change and 52 afterwards, the improvement is 12 cases, or 30 per cent, but only if the other conditions were broadly similar. If staff numbers had also risen, the improvement cannot be credited entirely to the change. Say so briefly: this shows honest thinking. Watch for unintended consequences too. A faster process that produces more errors is not an improvement, so measure quality as well as speed. For example, a clerk who shortens a form finds that processing time falls from ten minutes to seven but that the number of returned forms rises. She adds a short checklist, and the returns fall back. This shows she checked both speed and quality, and adjusted. Percentages should be calculated correctly: percentage change is the difference divided by the starting figure. Going from 10 minutes to 7 is a fall of 3 minutes, which is 30 per cent of 10. Do not exaggerate; a small, honest improvement beats an inflated claim. If you cannot measure, use other evidence such as complaints received, comments from users or the time colleagues report saving.

questions.prompt: Why is a baseline needed before a change?

options.text: It is required by law before any change to a process
Without one, a figure after the change means little
It makes the form longer, which gives a better result
It shows who is responsible for the change

questions.hint: You need something to compare with.

questions.prompt: Cases per day rose from 40 to 52. What is the percentage increase?

options.text: 12 per cent
23 per cent
52 per cent
30 per cent

questions.prompt: Processing time fell from 10 minutes to 7. What percentage fall is that?

options.text: 3 per cent
30 per cent
43 per cent
70 per cent

questions.prompt: Why should the candidate mention that staff numbers had risen?

options.text: It excuses a poor result
It reduces the claim to nothing
It shows honest thinking about what caused the improvement
It is required by the application form

questions.prompt: What is an unintended consequence in the shortened form example?

options.text: More returned forms
Faster processing of each form
A shorter form for the customer
A checklist for the clerk

questions.prompt: Why measure quality as well as speed?

options.text: Quality is easier to measure than speed
A faster process producing errors is not an improvement

items.title: L8: Delivering at Pace when priorities change
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Priorities change in most workplaces, and a strong Delivering at Pace answer shows how you cope. Typical changes include an urgent request that cuts across your plan, a colleague's absence that increases your workload, or a deadline moved forward. The sensible response has five steps: take stock of what you are now expected to do, check which tasks are truly urgent and consequential, agree with your manager what can wait, tell those affected about any delay, and replan. Agreeing with the manager matters because the choice about what to drop is often not yours alone. Consider an officer whose manager asks her on Wednesday to prepare figures for a meeting on Friday, in addition to her routine post. She estimates that the figures need six hours. She lists her week, finds that the post can be cleared in a shorter time if she handles the simple items only and passes the complex ones to a colleague with her manager's agreement, and tells two customers their replies will be a day later. She sends the figures on Thursday afternoon and clears the post by Monday. Notice the use of estimating, negotiating, communicating and meeting the date. Candidates sometimes describe saying yes to everything, which may look keen but rarely shows judgement. Equally poor is saying no with no alternative. Resilience also counts: staying calm, staying positive and learning from what happened. Afterwards, reflect briefly on what you would plan differently, for example asking for earlier notice.

items.title: L8: Giving feedback and coaching a peer
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Developing Others is stronger when the person shows how they helped someone else improve rather than simply telling them what to do. Coaching differs from instructing: a coach asks questions that help the other person think, whereas an instructor tells them the answer. Both have a place. When someone is new to a task, a clear demonstration is useful. When they have the basics but are making errors, questions such as 'What did you notice about that case?' help them find the cause. Giving feedback works best when it is prompt, specific and kind: describe what you saw, say what effect it had, and suggest what to try next. 'You did that badly' is not feedback. 'In that call you gave the date before you had checked the record, so the customer had to be called back; next time check first' is. After feedback, follow up to see whether it has helped. A peer might not be your direct report, so take care to be respectful and ask permission, for example 'Would it help if I shared something I noticed?'. A strong story might be: 'A colleague kept returning forms with the same two errors. I asked if she wanted a second pair of eyes, sat with her on three forms, asked what she noticed, and drew up a short checklist together. Her returns fell from six a week to one.' It shows listening, questioning, joint problem solving and a result. Also be willing to receive feedback yourself, which belongs to the same Behaviour.

items.title: L8: Strengths questions in different formats
items.body: Strengths questions can come in several formats. Some are open: 'What are you most proud of?' Some are paired choices: 'Would you rather work with data or with people?' Some are short and rapid, with only a few seconds to answer. Some are situational: 'You arrive and find the office has had a change of plan; what do you do first?'. Panels watch your tone and energy as well as your words. The aim is to hear what you naturally enjoy and do well, not to test what you have rehearsed. For paired choices, there is usually no right side, so choose the one that is true and give a short reason: 'People, because I like finding out what someone needs, though I enjoy data when it explains a pattern.' It is acceptable to say you enjoy both, but explain how. For rapid questions, a short answer is fine; do not fill the silence. If you say you love planning, you may be asked 'What do you do when the plan falls apart?', so be ready for honest follow-ups. Prepare by thinking about activities that give you energy, such as organising, helping others, learning new things or fixing problems, and look at the advert to see which of them fit the work. Avoid overclaiming. Saying you love detailed checking when you find it tedious will show when the panel asks about a task you disliked. You can also mention things you are still developing. This honesty gives the panel confidence that your answers are real.

items.title: L8: Scaling home and voluntary evidence for EO
items.body: An AO application can rely on one-to-one tasks, such as helping a relative with paperwork or running a till. EO evidence usually needs more: coordinating others, handling more than one demand at once, and dealing with problems that do not have a ready answer. If your experience is at home or voluntary, you can raise the scale by choosing the right example and describing it in the right terms. For instance, instead of 'I help at a food bank', an EO-level example might say: 'I coordinate eight volunteers each Saturday, arranging the rota, checking stock records against deliveries and resolving shortages by contacting donors.' Look for evidence of responsibility for others' work, decisions beyond your own tasks, handling exceptions, and effects on many people. Parent governors, club treasurers, school PTA officers, community organisers and neighbourhood committee members often have such evidence. Caring for several people, or managing complex arrangements with professionals, may also qualify. Do not invent scale; if you coordinated three people, say three. Instead of inflating, show depth. Describe a hard decision, a disagreement you resolved or a process you improved. Also note continuity. An activity done for several years, with changes made over time, shows commitment and learning. For roles at EO, using a mix of examples, one from paid work and one from voluntary work, is perfectly acceptable. Finally, link the example to the Behaviour in the question, not just to the grade, because a large example that does not fit the Behaviour will not score.
